data.title: OrbiMed Advisors Discloses Investment at Electra Therapeutics with 11.0% Stake
data.description:
OrbiMed Advisors LLC disclosed an 11.0% stake in Electra Therapeutics, Inc. common stock. The filing, dated September 25, 2026, follows Electra Therapeutics’ IPO and the conversion of preferred shares into common stock. The position reflects a significant life sciences investor taking a meaningful post-IPO stake.

Investor Intent

OrbiMed states it bought the shares for investment and "not with the intention of acquiring control" of Electra Therapeutics. The firm says it has no current plans for mergers, asset sales, board changes, or other corporate actions, but it may buy or sell shares in the future.

The group agreed to a 180-day lock-up after the IPO, saying it will "not sell or offer to sell" its shares during that period, subject to limited exceptions. OrbiMed and affiliated funds also hold registration rights that allow them to request future public resale registrations after IPO lock-up windows expire and other conditions are met.

Investor's Background

OrbiMed Advisors LLC is a Delaware limited liability company and a registered investment adviser focused on healthcare and life sciences. The firm invests globally across venture capital, private equity, and public equities in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and medical devices. OrbiMed is known for backing drug development companies through late-stage clinical milestones and for active engagement with boards.

Original SEC Filing: Electra Therapeutics, Inc. [ ETRA ] - SCHEDULE 13D - Sep. 25, 2026

data.title: Southland Receives Notice of Noncompliance with NYSE American Continued Listing Standards
data.description:
On September 23, 2026, Southland Holdings, Inc. (NYSE American: SLND and SLND WS) (the “Company”) received notification (the “Notice”) from NYSE Regulation of the NYSE American LLC (“NYSE American”) that the Company is no longer in compliance with NYSE American’s continued listing standards. Specifically, the Notice states that the Company is not in compliance with the continued listing standards set forth in Sections 1003(a)(i) and 1003(a)(ii) of the NYSE American Company Guide (the “Company Guide”). Section 1003(a)(i) requires a listed company to have stockholders’ equity of $2.0 million or more if the listed company has reported losses from continuing operations and/or net losses in two of its three most recent fiscal years. Section 1003(a)(ii) requires a listed company to have stockholders’ equity of $4.0 million or more if the listed company has reported losses from continuing operations and/or net losses in three of its four most recent fiscal years. The Company reported stockholders’ deficit of $248.2 million at June 30, 2026, and had reported net losses in its last three fiscal years. The Company is also not currently eligible for any exemption in Section 1003(a) of the Company Guide from the stockholders’ equity requirements.

The Company must submit a plan by October 23, 2026, advising NYSE Regulation of actions the Company has taken or will take to regain compliance with the continued listing standards by March 23, 2028. The Notice has no immediate impact on the listing of the Company’s shares of common stock and warrants, which will continue to be listed and traded on the NYSE American under the symbols “SLND” and “SLND WS,” respectively, during this period, subject to the Company’s compliance with the other listing requirements of the NYSE American.

The Company intends to submit a plan to NYSE Regulation by October 23, 2026, outlining the actions it has taken or intends to take to regain compliance with the continued listing standards. If NYSE Regulation accepts the Company’s plan, the Company expects to be able to continue its listing during the plan period and will be subject to continued periodic review by the NYSE Regulation staff. If the Company does not submit a plan or if the plan is not accepted, delisting proceedings will commence. Furthermore, if the plan is accepted but the Company is not in compliance with the continued listing standards by March 23, 2028, or if the Company does not make progress consistent with the plan during the plan period, NYSE Regulation staff will initiate delisting proceedings as appropriate. The Company may appeal a staff delisting determination in accordance with Section 1010 and Part 12 of the Company Guide. The receipt of the Notice does not affect the Company’s business operations or its reporting obligations with the SEC.

About Southland

Southland is a leading provider of specialized infrastructure construction services. With roots dating back to 1900, Southland and its subsidiaries form one of the largest infrastructure construction companies in North America, with experience throughout the world. The company serves the bridges, tunneling, communications, data centers, transportation and facilities, marine, steel structures, water and wastewater treatment, and water pipeline end markets. Southland is headquartered in Grapevine, Texas.

Forward-Looking Statements

This press release contains, and Southland’s officers and representatives may from time to time make, “forward-looking statements” within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the U.S. Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements can be identified by words such as “believe,” “continue,” “expect,” “may,” “plan,” “future,” “will,” “would,” and similar references to future periods. data.title: S&P signals Czech rating upgrade in 15 years as resilient economy weathers headwinds
data.description:
Global ratings agency S&P revised the Czech Republic's outlook to "positive" from "stable" on Friday, citing increased likelihood for the country's economy to withstand external headwinds.

"The outlook revision to positive reflects Czechia's continued economic convergence process with higher-income peers. We expect the Czech economy to remain resilient in the face of external challenges," S&P said in a statement.

S&P's outlook revision has brought the sovereign a step closer to a potential upgrade, with the agency last lifting the Czech Republic's rating in August 2011.

The country has maintained lower deficits than its peers in central and eastern Europe, keeping below the European Union-mandated ceiling of 3% of gross domestic product, a level which Andrej Babis' cabinet also pledged to keep in its programme manifesto.

The move also comes days after the Babis government, which took office last year, approved a 2027 draft budget that is set to widen the deficit for a third straight year to keep up with Babis' pledges to raise spending on public wages, road investments, healthcare and defence.

S&P maintained the nation's long-term 'AA-' foreign currency and 'AA' local currency sovereign credit ratings.

data.title: What China Really Wants From the U.S., According to Kevin Rudd — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Andy Serwer

With China's leader Xi Jinping wrapping his three-day visit with President Donald Trump in the U.S. on Friday, the question is what was achieved and what did each side want to get out of the bilateral summit?

To answer the former, the answer is not much, beyond extending the U.S.-China trade truce-previously scheduled to expire Nov. 10-by two months to January 2027. What each side wanted is a more complex question-and one I put to Kevin Rudd, the former prime minister of Australia, a fluent Mandarin speaker who has spent decades working in China.

Rudd, the former ambassador to the U.S. and current CEO of the educational nonprofit Asia Society, spoke with me in a Thursday interview at Journal House on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

His comments have been edited and condensed for clarity.

Barron's: What did the Chinese want from this meeting?

Kevin Rudd: Number one, they want a summit without any political or protocol glitch. Why? Because this is all about China and its domestic media. If you follow it as closely, Xi Jinping being treated as a coequal as the president of the U.S. and therefore sending the symbolism to the Chinese audience back home and around the world that China is now on the same level as America. That's the deep narrative in the Chinese propaganda stakes. And that's not to be underestimated.

There must be some more substantive things, no?

From the Chinese lens, I would say: tariffs, tariffs, and tariffs. Because if you look carefully at the Chinese economic model at the moment, much of it is not working. China's private domestic consumption is flat. China's private fixed capital investment growth is flat. China's private residential construction is now into its sixth year of recession. The only pistons working in this engine at the moment are one, state investment or state driven investment in its techno-industrial sector.

Secondly, on top of that net exports which is a big driver. China is earning $1.2 to $1.3 trillion from the rest of the world. What China can least afford, therefore, going into the summit in Washington, is for there to be a snapback in tariffs or a tariff increase on those pre-existing arrangements, which U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is perfectly empowered to do. The Chinese want that to be controlled and contained.

The U.S. believed it had an agreement with the Chinese and Xi Jinping in Busan last year to normalize trade in critical minerals and rare earths. China has moved to normalize that, except for two countries in the world: the U.S. and Japan. The Chinese are deliberately using this as leverage. What leverage are they trying to apply? They want to get the Americans to further reduce export controls on critical technology exports to China, most particularly advanced semiconductors.

What does the U.S. want?

For the Chinese to honor the Busan Agreement and fully normalize critical minerals and rare earths, and if they don't, then the real risk from the Chinese lens is that America, through a whole bunch of other partners in the world, including Australia, will simply move to plug this gap over the course of the next two to three years, and China's leverage then disappears. So, President Donald Trump wants this one fixed, plus a huge addition to China's currently constrained agricultural imports from the United States. Given, of course, the pain that's inflicted.

Extending the life of the current tariff pause by two months is basically sending a signal to Beijing, 'We expect this to be fixed by Christmas. If not, be on notice that we can go to a tariff increase, maybe even leverage the Europeans to increase tariffs.'

So you're saying that they want, say Nvidia chips, and we want their critical minerals?

The president's lens on this is, 'Hey we'll keep tariffs lower than they would otherwise be, but you need to honor your side of the bargain, which is to fully normalize critical minerals and rare earths exports, or alternatively, we'll bring tariffs right back up and maybe increase them further.'

More broadly, what does China want over time, and exactly how weak or strong is the economy? I go to China and things look okay to me.

On the surface, most things do look okay in China, but look at rising youth unemployment. That is a massive problem in terms of the Chinese demographic, and then social stability and therefore ultimately political stability, and that's before Chinese manufacturing and the total economy has fully absorbed and diffused artificial intelligence. Because as we know, one of the productivity yields of AI is labor force reduction in labor-intensive industries. This is the global center of robotics. What happens to all those folks who have been working on assembly lines across China for the last 20 or 30 years? Below the surface the Chinese have a bunch of economic problems.

How strong are they? What Xi Jinping has sought to build is a strong China. He says that Mao Zedong caused China to stand up, Deng Xiaoping caused China to become rich or richer. Under Xi Jinping, we're making China strong, and that goes back to the narrative about coequal strength with the U.S. militarily, beyond the drivers of the economy, including technology. Militarily the Chinese are doing well. They now have the largest surface fleet in the world.

Bigger than the U. S.?

Last count earlier this year was something in the order of 370 to 390 surface combatants in the PLA Navy against 270 to 290 here in the United States. The U.S. submarine force is slightly ahead and certainly further ahead in terms of the qualitative superiority of U.S. submarines, including nuclear-powered attack-class submarines.

Are there different measures of Chinese national power?

The Chinese internal calculus is called comprehensive national power, and they factor in the economy, technology, the military, and other associated assets. If you look carefully at their public commentary year by year under Xi Jinping, they're saying this is getting better and better. So their strategic calculus is that they will emerge more powerful than America.

I think there's a problem with that analysis because it underestimates the ability for America to reinvent itself, for which Silicon Valley is a classic example about how you constantly make things new in this country. So I think the Chinese may be having a fit of premature hubris, and that's dangerous because it can give rise to excessive political self-confidence.

So is that the endgame, Kevin? Or would that be manifested in eventually taking Taiwan in some way, shape, or form?

If you ask me to summarize what the Chinese worldview is, it is that strength is for a purpose. It's not an endpoint in itself. But remember, the underlying political culture of the People's Republic of China is that it's a Marxist-Leninist state, where power proceeds from the barrel of a gun, as Mao Zedong said. Lenin was not a liberal democrat. Stalin was not a liberal democrat. Mao was not a liberal democrat, nor is Xi Jinping a liberal democrat. It's an axiom which proceeds from the power of the state, the power of the military, the power of the security apparatus.

So what's the endpoint? Grounded in that power, China's core objective is to, as they would say, reunify the country. Taiwan has been absent from the Chinese political union since 1949. Xi Jinping would dearly love to complete the reunification project. If you look at China's military preparedness for this, together with their other territorial claims, maritime territorial claims primarily in East Asia, against Japan, against the Philippines, against Vietnam, and against Korea, that's where China wants to land. Second, to then become the dominant military and economic power in the East Asian Hemisphere, so that they are the power principle of the wider region.

And then, globally, you look carefully at Xi Jinping's plans for the reform of global governance, and he has these four grand initiatives: the Global Civilization Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Development Initiative and the Global Governance Initiative, as well as the Belt and Road Initiative, this is all designed toward creating a new architecture where the U.S. is no longer its center, but China is.

I was going to ask about that. In other words, 'Okay, China, that's your view of the world. Where does the U.S. fit in?' Do they want a bipolar world, for instance, or do they want to just get rid of us completely.

As I look at the operational characteristics of Chinese strategy on the ground in the Indo-Pacific, it's to push the U.S. back to the Central Pacific, because they would see East Asia and the Western Pacific as their natural hemisphere, their natural sphere of influence. Think of the historical evolution of the Monroe Doctrine in the Western Hemisphere, and the Chinese have been active students of the Monroe Doctrine and its evolution over time. That is the play.

Secondly, in the declaratory policy of Xi Jinping, and I looked at his language on arrival at Joint Base Andrews, where he said, 'Make America great again,' and the great renaissance of the Chinese people-which is his signature call to China since he became president, which is China returning to the power it had in the world prior to the Opium Wars-these are not incompatible. There's no contradiction between them. That's his declaratory position.

I'm less confident of that being the operational reality, because if you go to the meat and potatoes of the AI competition at the moment, President Donald Trump says in black and white, 'He who wins AI, wins.' He sees this as a fairly binary competition with the U.S. in terms of this future driver of both economic and military power. Xi Jinping's narrative internally is much the same.

data.title: Small-Cap Stocks Are Struggling. The Case for Going Even Smaller. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Teresa Rivas

When it comes to small-cap stocks, investors might want to go really small or go home.

Small-caps have had a tough time recently. The Russell 2000 is down more than 4% over the past month as of the end of Friday trading, outpacing the Dow Jones Industrial Average's 2.6% decline. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite have risen 0.8% and 2.7% over the same period.

That makes sense, because the market has been anticipating an interest-rate increase for some time, and the Federal Reserve finally delivered one earlier this month. Smaller companies naturally tend to have less cash on hand and less access to financing. That leaves them especially sensitive to higher interest rates, which increase the costs of taking on debt they might need to grow.

In fact, small-caps have underperformed the S&P 500 since August, and that pattern could continue, 22V Research President and Chief Market Strategist Dennis DeBusschere, says.

Small-caps have historically struggled when megacaps are in vogue, so as long as companies like the Magnificent Seven capture all the investor attention, there's less cash to spare for smaller stocks.

There are concerns about the potential slowdown in artificial intelligence development, but AI and tech are where the most earnings growth is. That means investors keep favoring the sector, which is full of extra-large companies. The Nasdaq is easily the best-performing index over the past month, rising more than 2%, and it's climbed for two weeks straight.

The macroeconomic backdrop is another headwind for small-caps, DeBusschere writes, as history shows they have typically lagged behind large-caps at the beginning of interest-rate hike cycles. But that advantage erodes eventually, with small-caps more likely to mount a comeback over the six- or 12-month periods. Still, where we stand now-at the start of the cycle-is toughest for the group.

As a result, fundamentals are increasingly important to a small-cap stocks' performance during times like these. But they're behind the eight ball in that area, too, DeBusschere says, adding that small-cap companies' margins are below those of mid- and large-cap companies.

So while there is historical evidence that small-caps can recover, he's skeptical of their near-term prospects.

That said, for investors who do want exposure to that part of the market, really leaning into the theme-by going big on the smallest companies-might be one way to go.

After all, the Russell 2000's 14% rise year to date is ahead of the S&P 500's gain, but micro caps have shone even brighter. So far in 2026, the iShares Micro-Cap exchange-traded fund and the DFA US Micro Cap Portfolio ETF have done even better, both rising roughly 18%. That is even ahead of the Nasdaq's 16.5% gain this year. It's true that microcaps have also notched losses over the past month, but they could come back stronger if they revert to the pattern of outperformance seen earlier this year.

"Some of the tailwinds behind their recent rally include momentum, increasing speculative behavior, superb earnings growth, outsize gains for certain AI/energy/ biotech-related stocks, reshoring, and tax incentives," Sevens Report President Tom Essaye writes.

He admits that microcaps are sensitive to interest-rate increases just like small-caps, but there are tailwinds for them, too. Without much in the way of Wall Street coverage or news flow, there is a greater chance to find undervalued hidden gems, while micro caps tend to have high levels of insider ownership-one indicator of stock outperformance. They also tend to be less correlated to other parts of the market, making them ideal for diversification. Plus, many are takeover candidates that can be bought out by larger companies, potentially at a premium.

"Generally speaking, microcaps tend to march to the beat of their own drum," Essaye concludes. "But I think if liquidity is high and the environment is risk-on, microcaps can continue to outperform."

Some companies may be small but mighty.

Write to Teresa Rivas at teresa.rivas@barrons.com

data.title: Brazil's Lula bans online betting operations as reelection race tightens
data.description:
Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Friday announced a ban on online betting operations in Latin America's largest economy, the latest in a series of measures unveiled ahead of next month's election.

The move came as opinion polls have shown Lula locked in a tight race with right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, ahead of the October 4 first-round vote.

The executive order bans online betting operations in Brazil less than two years after the government kicked off a legal framework allowing the industry to operate. It takes immediate effect but must be approved by Congress within 120 days to remain in force.

The crackdown reflects growing concern within the government that rising spending on gambling has drained household budgets and contributed to record levels of indebtedness. Recent surveys showed roughly three-quarters of Brazilians support a complete ban on online betting.

"We are facing a public health issue involving online betting. It is a serious problem," said Finance Minister Dario Durigan during the announcement.

Senator Bolsonaro called the measure "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday.

data.title: New York Sues Polymarket Over Alleged Illegal Gambling Operation
data.description:
Key points:
  • New York Attorney General Letitia James and Governor Kathy Hochul have announced a lawsuit against Polymarket US.
  • The state alleges the prediction platform is operating illegal, unlicensed gambling in New York.
  • The lawsuit seeks to stop the activity and asks for fines, forfeiture of alleged illegal gains and restitution for users.

**ID:** N25-03

**Site:** NewsBTC

**Status:** READY

**Author:** NewsBTC Editorial Team

**Focus Keyword:** Polymarket

**Image Keyword:** Regulation

**Category:** Regulation

**Tags:** Polymarket, New York, Prediction Markets, Regulation, Kalshi

**Primary Source:** https://ag.ny.gov/press-release

New York Says The Federal Structure Does Not Override State Gambling Law

Polymarket returned to the U.S. market after acquiring regulated exchange infrastructure and operating under the federal commodities framework.

New York is arguing that this does not give the platform a free pass under state gambling rules.

According to the Attorney General’s office, an investigation found that Polymarket offered users the ability to wager on sporting events without a New York gambling license.

The state also alleges the platform exposes users below New York’s legal gambling age of 21 to those markets.

The lawsuit asks a court to block Polymarket from continuing to operate what the state describes as an unlicensed gambling business.

It also seeks financial penalties, forfeiture of alleged illegal proceeds and restitution.

Prediction Markets Are Running Into A Jurisdiction Problem

The dispute highlights a structural problem that has followed prediction markets as they expand.

At the federal level, event contracts can fall under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

At the state level, regulators can look at exactly the same product and see a wager.

Sports contracts make that conflict particularly sharp.

A market on inflation or an election may be framed as a forecasting or hedging instrument.

A contract paying out on the result of a basketball game can look much closer to conventional sports betting.

The New York lawsuit does not establish that Polymarket has broken the law; those allegations now have to be tested in court.

But it raises the stakes considerably.

Prediction markets have grown from a crypto curiosity into a substantial consumer product.

As that happens, the industry’s biggest challenge may not be finding users.

It may be convincing federal and state regulators that everyone agrees on what these markets actually are.

*This article was written by the News Desk and edited by [Samuel Rae](https://www.newsbtc.com/author/rae-samuel/).*

data.title: NU E Power Corp. Closes Shares for Debt Settlement
data.description:
Calgary, Alberta and Vancouver, British Columbia--(Newsfile Corp. - September 25, 2026) - NU E Power Corp. (OTC Pink: NUEPF) (FSE: NUE1) ("NUE" or the "Company") announces that, further to its news release of September 10, 2026, it has issued 700,000 units at a deemed price of $0.15 per unit to Cronin Capital Corp. in settlement of a bona fide debt of $105,000. data.title: U.S. Bond Market Wraps Up Tumultuous Week — WSJ
data.description:
By WSJ Staff

The 10-year Treasury yield jumped 0.185 percentage point this week to a level not seen since 2007.

  • It was the fourth consecutive week of yield increases for the benchmark 10-year Treasury and its 10th weekly increase over the past 13 weeks, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
  • The 2-year Treasury yield has an even longer weekly streak going. It ended the week 0.121 percentage point higher than it started. That represents the sixth straight week of increases. During that period, the yield has risen 0.692 percentage point, the sharpest move in more than three years.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).
